items.title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Within a few hours of each other (timeline), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics (Scientific American). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human, work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible, and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable. Sponsored by Agentfield.AIOpen models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix.Try CodeAF! As Levent eloquently put it: “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter: The nature of Slop: Levent says “I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around
items.why_it_matters: A Claude-driven, Lean-formalized Riemann Hypothesis proof would be a big signal of what frontier models can do on long, verifiable reasoning. It's interesting for AI-product clients, but it has little direct effect on day-to-day delivery.

items.title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
items.author: LetThingsBeDiff
items.excerpt: I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50583761 Points: 581 # Comments: 636

items.title: llm-gemini 0.38.1
items.excerpt: Release: llm-gemini 0.38.1 Gemini 4 Carbon only supports low, medium and high reasoning levels - but Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Neon both have an extra xhigh level. I missed that when I added those models to the llm-gemini plugin, which is now fixed in this dot release. The xhigh setting for Hydrogen makes a significant difference. I updated my Gemini 4 comparison grid - note how Hydrogen at high used 5,311 output tokens and cost 3.99 cents, but the same model at xhigh used 31,477 output tokens, cost 23.61 cents, and produced a pelican that's competitive with Gemini 4 Neon: Tags: gemini, llm, llm-reasoning, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai, llms, google, generative-ai
items.why_it_matters: Shows the extra xhigh reasoning level on Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Neon and what it costs: about 6x the tokens and price. That's useful when choosing Gemini API settings for client features.

items.title: Muru
items.excerpt: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. Tags: graham-dumpleton, modwsgi, python, wsgi, ai, rust, asgi, generative-ai, llms, ai-assisted-programming
items.why_it_matters: A new AI-assisted Rust server for Python ASGI and WSGI apps, with a detailed public build log. It could matter for Python ML serving and is a useful example of documented AI-assisted development.
